title: Last stand at Tebourba

facts.text: In late November 1942, less than three weeks after the Torch landings, British and American columns raced east for Tunis. By 28 November British troops held a ridge above Djedeida, on the plain that runs down to the city, some twelve miles away.
On the night of 29 November the 2nd Battalion, The Hampshire Regiment, newly arrived in Africa, took over the line in front of Djedeida, east of Tebourba.
At 7.45 a.m. on 1 December the Germans struck back. General Wolfgang Fischer's 10th Panzer Division led the counterattack, with parachute infantry of Group Koch pinning the Allies further south.
The Hampshires held their ridge. The U.S. Army's official history says their stubborn resistance held the attackers far short of their objective.

American tanks of Combat Command B, 1st Armored Division, joined the fight. On 2 December a sortie by light tanks of the 13th Armored Regiment was driven back; outgunned and mired off the road, nineteen were lost.

On the afternoon of 3 December the Germans took a high feature on the Hampshires' flank. Counterattacks failed. Major Herbert Wallace Le Patourel, 26, then led four volunteers up the hill under very heavy fire and silenced several machine gun posts.
When the rest of his party had all been killed or wounded, Le Patourel went forward alone with a pistol and some grenades to attack the machine guns at close quarters. He did not come back.
That night the survivors pulled out under fire along a track by the river, abandoning guns and vehicles and escaping across country in small groups. Tebourba fell at 11 a.m. on 4 December.

The Hampshires lost 495 men, about 72 percent of the battalion. Their brigade's three battalions were reduced to about 660 men, plus stragglers. Fischer claimed 55 tanks and more than 1,000 prisoners in four days.
On 9 March 1943 the London Gazette announced Le Patourel's Victoria Cross as a posthumous award. Based on reports from wounded men, the citation said he had died of wounds.
He had not. A correction in the next week's Gazette deleted the word posthumous: he was a prisoner of war. Badly wounded and captured, he was repatriated in 1943 and received his Cross in Cairo.
The Allies had come within about twelve miles of Tunis. They did not get there until 7 May 1943, five months after Tebourba.

Major General Vyvyan Evelegh, commander of the British 78th Infantry Division (whose 11th Brigade the Hampshires fought beside at Tebourba), in the forward area on 5 December 1942, the day after Tebourba fell. IWM NA 201, Sgt Frederick Wackett, No. 2 Army Film and Photographic Unit, Crown copyright expired, PD UKGov on Commons. The Commons copy is only 800 x 540 (IWM uploads are capped); saved upscaled. declassified.fact: Le Patourel was born in Guernsey in 1916. When he won the Victoria Cross, his home island had been under German occupation since 1940. He stayed in the Army after the war, rose to brigadier, and his Cross is now at the Royal Hampshire Regiment Museum in Winchester.

film.shot_notes: Whole reel 3, 9 min 44 s, narration and score, run silent. NARA: reel 3 shows Allied troops entering Tunisia, capturing Beja and Medjez el Bab, reaching toward Tunis and withdrawing under counterattacks, and a tank battle. 06:16 to 06:30 German film of a German machine gunner (avoid, or caption it as German film from the U.S. film); 06:40 a Stuart tank and infantry; 06:48 the Beja sign; 07:04 a British general at a map; 07:12 troops past a cafe; NOON: 07:18 to 07:52, half tracks and tanks moving across open country, smoke rising over armor (07:36), a gun crew (07:44), a fire at night (07:52). Open on the half track at 07:18 or the smoke over the tanks at 07:36. 08:00 animated map (avoid). Tunisian Victory includes some reenacted scenes; the Film Library index lists them, so the Thursday cut should check this stretch against it (Medjez el Bab is indexed at 06:39 to 07:24).
film.date_note: Film of the Allied drive on Tunis, late November to early December 1942, not dated to 1 December or to Tebourba itself. Caption as British and American film of the drive on Tunis, late 1942, from Tunisian Victory (1944).
